title: Bayesian measurement design and information gain

items.title: Design-indexed dominated inverse experiment
items.statement:
Let $D$ be a finite set of design indices, let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be measurable spaces, let $\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let $\nu$ be a sigma-finite measure on $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$. For each $d\in D$, let $Q_d$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta$ to $\mathsf Y$ with a specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $p_d(y\mid\theta)$ relative to $\nu$, so
$$Q_d(\theta,B)=\int_B p_d(y\mid\theta)\,\nu(dy)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Define the prior-predictive density $p_d(y)=\int_\Theta p_d(y\mid\theta)\,\mu_0(d\theta)$. For each datum $y$ with $0<p_d(y)<\infty$, define the posterior probability measure
$$\mu_d^y(A)=\frac{\int_A p_d(y\mid\theta)\,\mu_0(d\theta)}{p_d(y)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The dominated-kernel Bayes formula makes $p_d\,d\nu$ the observation law and identifies $\mu_d^y$ as a posterior version on these positive finite evidence fibers. No posterior formula is assigned on fibers with zero or infinite evidence; their prior-predictive probability is zero.

references.title: Kathryn Chaloner and Isabella Verdinelli, Bayesian Experimental Design: A Review, Statistical Science 10(3) (1995), 273–304
references.locator: §1.2, equations (1)–(2): expected utility under the prior-predictive distribution.

references.title: David J. C. MacKay, Information-Based Objective Functions for Active Data Selection, Neural Computation 4(4) (1992), 590–604

items.axiom_use: No choice axiom is used to specify the prior, dominated probability kernels, predictive densities, or positive-finite-evidence posterior fibers. The supplied dominated-kernel Bayes formula is choice-free.

items.title: Expected information gain
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice for the library's Kullback–Leibler divergence convention. For a design $d$ in a design-indexed dominated inverse experiment, let $G_d=\{y:0<p_d(y)<\infty\}$ be its positive finite evidence fibers. The **expected information gain** is
$$\operatorname{EIG}(d):=\int_{G_d}D(\mu_d^y\|\mu_0)\,p_d(y)\,\nu(dy)\in[0,+\infty],$$
where the integrand is defined to be zero outside $G_d$. Here $D(P\|Q)$ is the directional Kullback–Leibler divergence of probability measures, with natural logarithms.

references.title: Kathryn Chaloner and Isabella Verdinelli, Bayesian Experimental Design: A Review, Statistical Science 10(3) (1995), 273–304
references.locator: §2.2, equation (3): expected posterior-to-prior Kullback–Leibler distance as a design utility.

references.title: David J. C. MacKay, Information-Based Objective Functions for Active Data Selection, Neural Computation 4(4) (1992), 590–604
references.locator: §2, complete expected-information derivation under the model's prior-predictive distribution.

items.axiom_use: AC is inherited only through the library's general Radon–Nikodym-based Kullback–Leibler divergence convention. The explicit dominated densities and the extended nonnegative integral add no stronger choice principle.

items.title: Expected information gain is joint relative entropy
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a design $d$ in a design-indexed dominated inverse experiment, with prior $\mu_0$, likelihood density $p_d(y\mid\theta)$ relative to the common sigma-finite measure $\nu$, predictive density $p_d(y)$, and posterior $\mu_d^y$ on $G_d=\{y:0<p_d(y)<\infty\}$. Let $P_d$ be the joint law of $(\theta,Y)$, so on measurable rectangles
$$P_d(A\times B)=\int_B\int_Ap_d(y\mid\theta)\,\mu_0(d\theta)\,\nu(dy),$$
let $P_{Y\mid d}(B)=\int_Bp_d(y)\,\nu(dy)$, and let $Q_d=\mu_0\otimes P_{Y\mid d}$. Then
$$\operatorname{EIG}(d)=D(P_d\|Q_d)\in[0,+\infty].$$
On $G_d$, the Radon–Nikodym density $dP_d/dQ_d$ is $p_d(y\mid\theta)/p_d(y)$ almost everywhere. The identity is valid as an extended integral: its negative part is finite, its positive part may be infinite, and no subtraction of two infinite entropies occurs.

references.title: Kathryn Chaloner and Isabella Verdinelli, Bayesian Experimental Design: A Review, Statistical Science 10(3) (1995), 273–304
references.locator: §2.2, equation (3), expected posterior-to-prior KL criterion.

references.title: David J. C. MacKay, Information-Based Objective Functions for Active Data Selection, Neural Computation 4(4) (1992), 590–604

items.axiom_use: Assume AC only through the library's KL definition of a Radon–Nikodym derivative. The posterior density and all Tonelli, null-fiber, and integral exchanges in the proof use the supplied dominated densities and are choice-free.

items.title: Linear Gaussian information gain has a log-determinant formula
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$, let $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, let $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive semidefinite, let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, and let $\Gamma\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite. Suppose $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ and $\eta\sim N_m(0,\Gamma)$ are independent, and observe $Y=A\theta+\eta$. With $S=ACA^T+\Gamma$, the expected information gain of this experiment is
$$\operatorname{EIG}=\frac12\log\det\!\left(I_m+\Gamma^{-1/2}ACA^T\Gamma^{-1/2}\right).$$
Here $\Gamma^{-1/2}$ is the inverse of the unique symmetric positive-definite square root of $\Gamma$, and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The matrix inside the log determinant is positive definite. This formula permits singular $C$ and never uses differential entropy of $\theta$; the mean $m_0$ cancels. Noise depending on $\theta$ is outside the hypotheses and need not satisfy the formula.

references.title: Kathryn Chaloner and Isabella Verdinelli, Bayesian Experimental Design: A Review, Statistical Science 10(3) (1995), 273–304
references.locator: §2.2, normal-linear Bayesian D-optimality and its determinant criterion.

references.title: David J. C. MacKay, Information-Based Objective Functions for Active Data Selection, Neural Computation 4(4) (1992), 590–604
references.locator: §3.1, equations (3.4)–(3.6), Gaussian information gain from a determinant ratio.

references.title: Carl Edward Rasmussen and Christopher K. I. Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, MIT Press (2006)
references.locator: Chapter 2 §§2.1–2.2, finite Gaussian conditioning and predictive laws.

items.axiom_use: AC is inherited from the library KL convention, finite Gaussian and conditional-law interfaces. The expectation and finite matrix algebra in the local proof use no stronger choice principle and never require an inverse of the possibly singular state covariance.

items.title: Finite-candidate information design
items.statement:
Assume AC for the library KL/EIG convention. Input a prior covariance $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with $n\ge1$ symmetric positive semidefinite, a finite ordered list of raw candidate records $(A_d,\Gamma_d,c_d)_{d=1}^N$, and a real budget $B$. Each stored $A_d$ and $\Gamma_d$ is a finite real matrix, with its dimensions part of the input, and each declared cost $c_d$ is finite and real. A candidate is dimension-valid when $A_d$ has at least one row and exactly $n$ columns and $\Gamma_d$ is a symmetric square matrix whose dimension equals the row count of $A_d$; for a dimension-valid candidate write that common positive dimension as $m_d$. The prior mean is immaterial to the score.

Interpret each admissible candidate $d$ (dimension-valid with $\Gamma_d$ positive definite) as a separate singleton-design dominated inverse experiment with prior $\theta\sim N_n(m_0,C)$ for any $m_0\in\mathbb R^n$, observation space $\mathbb R^{m_d}$ with Lebesgue measure, and observation $Y_d=A_d\theta+\eta_d$, where $\eta_d\sim N_{m_d}(0,\Gamma_d)$ is independent of $\theta$. Here $\operatorname{EIG}(d)$ is the expected information gain from the preceding definition for that singleton experiment. Different candidates may have different $m_d$ because each is evaluated on its own observation space. The score is independent of $m_0$.

In exact-real arithmetic, process the list in order. Mark a candidate inadmissible if it is not dimension-valid or if its noise covariance $\Gamma_d$ is not positive definite. For each remaining candidate with $c_d\le B$, compute the Cholesky factor $\Gamma_d=L_dL_d^T$ with positive diagonal, solve $L_dV_d=A_d$ by forward substitution, and form the symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix $Z_d=V_dCV_d^T$. Set $H_d=I_{m_d}+Z_d$ and compute its Cholesky factor $H_d=R_dR_d^T$. Assign the utility
$$U_d=\sum_{j=1}^{m_d}\log (R_d)_{jj}-c_d=\tfrac12\log\det(H_d)-c_d.$$
Initialize the stored best candidate as unset. For each admissible candidate meeting the budget, set it if unset; otherwise replace it exactly when the new utility is strictly greater than the stored utility. After the scan, return the stored candidate. This update rule preserves the first index in any tie. If every candidate is inadmissible, return `all-inadmissible`; if at least one candidate is admissible but none meets the budget, return `budget-exhausted`.

In floating-point mode, use the failure-aware Cholesky and triangular-solve procedures. Certify the positive-definiteness status of every dimension-valid $\Gamma_d$; a failed rounded factorization alone is not evidence that $\Gamma_d$ is not positive definite. If any candidate's admissibility cannot be certified, return `numerically-unresolved`. Once admissibility is certified, return `all-inadmissible` if none is admissible and `budget-exhausted` if none meets the budget. Otherwise require a certified interval $[\widehat U_d-\varepsilon_d,\widehat U_d+\varepsilon_d]$ for each feasible candidate's exact utility. One admissible score certificate supplies a positive-semidefinite computed matrix $\widehat Z_d$ with $\|\widehat Z_d-Z_d\|_2\le\delta_d$, a successful computed Cholesky factor $\widehat R_d$ with $\|\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T-(I+\widehat Z_d)\|_2\le\rho_d<1$, and a remaining log/summation/cost evaluation radius $\lambda_d$. It sets
$$\varepsilon_d=\frac{m_d}{2}\left(\delta_d+\frac{\rho_d}{1-\rho_d}\right)+\lambda_d.$$
The matrix radius may be certified by the published information-matrix perturbation bound in its single-design, unit-weight $W=I$ case. Factor $C$ as $C^{1/2}C^{1/2}$ and set $J_d=C^{1/2}V_d^T$; for a computed solve $\widehat V_d$, set $\widehat J_d=C^{1/2}\widehat V_d^T$. Then $Z_d=J_d^TJ_d$ and $\widehat Z_d=\widehat J_d^T\widehat J_d$. The lemma's finite-design hypotheses hold for the one-point sensitivity maps $z\mapsto J_dz$ and $z\mapsto\widehat J_dz$ on $\mathbb R^{m_d}$, with weight $W=I$ and design weight $1$. If $\|J_d\|_2\le K_d$ and $\|\widehat J_d-J_d\|_2\le\eta_d$, then $\delta_d$ may be any verified bound at least $2K_d\eta_d+\eta_d^2$, enlarged by any separate matrix-formation residual. A rounded triangular-solve backward-error bound must be converted to the required forward matrix bound using verified conditioning; any rounding in the covariance-root multiply is included in $\eta_d$ or the formation residual. The published rounded-Cholesky and log-determinant perturbation results supply their stated components under their own hypotheses. A missing or failed certificate returns `numerically-unresolved` and no optimum claim. Given a comparison tolerance $\tau\ge0$, compute $M=\max_{d\text{ feasible}}\widehat U_d$ and return the first feasible candidate with $\widehat U_d\ge M-\tau$. Its true utility gap is at most $\tau+2\max_d\varepsilon_d$. If the selected candidate's lower interval endpoint exceeds every earlier candidate's upper endpoint and is at least every later candidate's upper endpoint, return it as the certified first exact maximizer. The algorithm makes no bit-complexity claim for exact-real comparisons.

references.locator: Chapter 2, Algorithm 2.1 and equation (2.30): Cholesky solves and log determinant from a positive-diagonal triangular factor.

references.title: Kathryn Chaloner and Isabella Verdinelli, Bayesian Experimental Design: A Review, Statistical Science 10(3) (1995), 273–304
references.locator: §2.2, expected information criterion in the normal linear model.

items.axiom_use: The finite scan and its deterministic tie rule are choice-free. The exact utility inherits AC from the EIG/KL convention; no arbitrary selection among the finite candidates is made.

items.title: Finite-candidate information design returns an exact or certified approximate optimum
items.statement:
Assume AC for the library KL/EIG convention.

Assume the finite-candidate algorithm's hypotheses. A candidate is admissible when it is dimension-valid and its symmetric noise covariance is positive definite; let $\mathcal V$ be the ordered list of admissible candidates and let $\mathcal F=(d\in\mathcal V:c_d\le B)$ in the inherited order. For each $d\in\mathcal F$, let $U_d=\operatorname{EIG}(d)-c_d$ be its exact utility. In exact-real mode, if $\mathcal F$ is nonempty, the algorithm returns the first index in $\mathcal F$ attaining $\max_{d\in\mathcal F}U_d$; if $\mathcal V$ is empty it returns `all-inadmissible`, and if $\mathcal V$ is nonempty but $\mathcal F$ is empty it returns `budget-exhausted`.

For the floating-point mode, suppose each $d\in\mathcal F$ has a computed score $\widehat U_d$, a symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix $\widehat Z_d$, a successful factor $\widehat R_d$, and certified radii $\delta_d\ge0$, $0\le\rho_d<1$, and $\lambda_d\ge0$ such that
$$\|\widehat Z_d-Z_d\|_2\le\delta_d,\qquad \|\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T-(I_{m_d}+\widehat Z_d)\|_2\le\rho_d,$$
where $Z_d$ is the exact Cholesky-whitened matrix in the algorithm's Definition, and
$$\left|\widehat U_d-\left(\frac12\log\det(\widehat R_d\widehat R_d^T)-c_d\right)\right|\le\lambda_d.$$
For example, the matrix-radius component can use the information-matrix perturbation result in its single-design, unit-weight $W=I$ specialization: if $Z_d=J_d^TJ_d$, $\widehat Z_d=\widehat J_d^T\widehat J_d$, $\|J_d\|_2\le K_d$, and $\|\widehat J_d-J_d\|_2\le\eta_d$, then $\delta_d\ge2K_d\eta_d+\eta_d^2$ is sufficient, with any separate formation residual added. A rounded triangular-solve backward-error bound must be converted to the needed forward matrix error using a verified conditioning bound. The rounded-Cholesky residual must follow from a successful factorization under its stated floating-point assumptions; in particular, the cited bound assumes $m u<1/5$, where $m=20m_d+20$ and $u$ is unit roundoff. The value $\lambda_d$ must bound the rounded logarithms, their summation, and cost evaluation. Set $\varepsilon_d=\frac{m_d}{2}\left(\delta_d+\frac{\rho_d}{1-\rho_d}\right)+\lambda_d$. If the algorithm returns a candidate $\widehat d$ with $\widehat U_{\widehat d}\ge\max_{d\in\mathcal F}\widehat U_d-\tau$, then
$$\max_{d\in\mathcal F}U_d-U_{\widehat d}\le\tau+\varepsilon_{d^*}+\varepsilon_{\widehat d}\le\tau+2\max_{d\in\mathcal F}\varepsilon_d,$$
where $d^*$ is any exact maximizer. If the certified score intervals show that the selected candidate's lower endpoint exceeds every earlier candidate's upper endpoint and is at least every later candidate's upper endpoint, it is the first exact maximizer. The matrix and factor radii must be certified under the published solve, information-matrix, rounded-Cholesky, and log-determinant error hypotheses; $\lambda_d$ must additionally cover rounded logarithm, summation, and cost evaluation.

title: Bayesian measurement design and information gain — Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Expected information gain under a wrong operator does not identify the operator-parameter pair
items.statement: The following implication is false: in every finite dominated inverse experiment, if expected information gain for a parameter is positive under a fixed nominal forward operator, then an unknown truth-operator pair is identifiable from the observation law, where identifiable means that distinct pairs induce distinct conditional observation laws.

references.title: David J. C. MacKay, Information-Based Objective Functions for Active Data Selection, Neural Computation 4(4) (1992), 590–604
references.locator: §6.1 and Conclusion: information utility is evaluated under the assumed model and can answer the wrong question when that model is incorrect.

references.locator: §1.2 and §2.2: the design objective averages information under the specified prior-predictive model.

items.title: Sensor placement along a high prior-variance direction
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $\theta\sim N_2(0,C)$ with $C=\operatorname{diag}(9,1)$. Compare two zero-cost one-sensor designs with independent unit-variance Gaussian noise: $d_1$ observes $A_1\theta$ with $A_1=(1,0)$, and $d_2$ observes $A_2\theta$ with $A_2=(0,1)$. Their expected information gains are $\frac12\log 10$ and $\frac12\log 2$, respectively, so the sensor measuring the higher prior-variance direction is uniquely preferred.

items.title: Repeated measurements with correlated noise
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $\theta\sim N(0,1)$ and take two repeated observations with $A=(1,1)^T$ and noise covariance $\Gamma_\rho=\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix}$, where $-1<\rho<1$. The matrix $\Gamma_\rho$ is positive definite. The expected information gain is $\frac12\log\left(1+\frac{2}{1+\rho}\right)$. In particular, correlation $\rho=\frac12$ gives $\frac12\log(7/3)$, less than the independent-noise value $\frac12\log 3$ at $\rho=0$.

items.title: Information gain on a singular prior support
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $\theta\sim N_2(0,C)$ with $C=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, so its support is the first coordinate axis. With unit-variance Gaussian noise, compare the one-coordinate measurements $A_\perp=(0,1)$ and $A_\parallel=(1,0)$. Their expected information gains are $0$ and $\frac12\log 2$, respectively. The log-determinant formula remains defined although $C$ is singular.
